answer:
Price caps took off in the mail in August 2000, and Jeff Dasovich wrote about them most. The counts below come from exact-phrase matching on "price cap" and "price caps".

**When**
- The mail_counts tool shows 923 matching emails overall, first seen on 2000-02-09. There were only a handful through June 2000, then 13 in July 2000, 44 in August and 48 in September.
- Weekly counts stayed at 1–5 until the week ending 2000-07-23. They rose to 8–10 a week in early August and hit 17 in the week ending 2000-09-03.
- Volume peaked in November and December 2000 (81 and 83). That was when FERC proposed and then adopted a "soft" cap.
- A second wave ran from spring 2001. May and June 2001 were the highest months, at 108 and 107 emails. Counts fell sharply after July 2001.
- The August 2000 rise followed the San Diego rate crisis. On 3 August, SDG&E's complaint "seeks $250 price caps against sellers into Cal. with market based rates."
- The same week, the CPUC voted 5-0 to reject instituting retail rate caps in San Diego.
- Earlier, in July, a press item had already covered a possible new ISO vote on a power price cap cut. That is the first visible sign.
- By 10 August, Dasovich reported that a Lynch proposed decision would reverse that rejection and set an "interim" retail rate cap for SDG&E.
- On 24 August, FERC denied San Diego's request to cap all California power sellers' rates at $250.

**Who wrote most**
- Among people's own emails (source "mail"), the top senders were:
  - Jeff Dasovich: 73
  - pmadpr@worldnet.att.net: 39
  - Mary Hain: 31
  - Alan Comnes: 24
  - Steven Kean: 22
  - rcarroll@bracepatt.com: 20
  - Susan Mara: 20
- Dasovich also led in the 2000 rise (July–Dec 2000: Dasovich 41, Hain 27, Mara 17, Kean 17). He led again in the 2001 wave (March–July 2001: Dasovich 19, pmadpr 16, Kristin Walsh 15, Comnes 14).
- Dasovich's own count peaked in November 2000 at 15 emails.
- His writing was tracking events and shaping Enron's position. On 1 November he wrote that FERC had declared the ISO Board's cap "null and void," so "we're back to the old $250 cap," with a "soft" $150 cap proposed to take effect in 60 days.
- On 7 November he relayed message points for the generators' association: "Price caps have failed in the past and they'll fail again," and that the cap proposal "is flawed."

**Caveats**
- The sender counts cover only emails containing the exact phrase "price cap" or "price caps." Mail that said "bid cap" or "rate cap" is not counted.
- Some top senders, such as the SCIENTECH issue alerts and the pmadpr sender, appear to be forwarding outside commentary or press. That may not reflect Enron staff's own views, and I didn't open pmadpr's emails.
- The August 2000 context comes from internal emails and forwarded press (Dow Jones, SF Examiner and SF Chronicle articles).

citations.cited_text:
Mary has this.  Seeks $250 price caps against sellers into Cal. with market 
based rates.

As you are probably aware, the CPUC voted 5-0 to reject instituting retail 
rate caps in San Diego and instead adopted SDG&E's proposal to refund over 
$100 million.  The Commission also approved SCE and PG&E's motion to enter 
into bilateral agreements and schedule those transactions through the PX 
using the bilateral-option market.  These transactions will be confidential 
and will be disclosed only to the Commission's energy division, for purposes 
of reasonableness.  The Commission did not act upon San Diego's advice letter 
(#1242) to facilitate customer awareness of competitive alternatives.  That 
advice letter will not be acted upon until the next Commission meeting in 
September.

Subject: Reuters -- Calif. ISO may vote again on power price cap cut
From: Tracey Bradley

In other late-breaking news.  On the heels of this press conference, I 
received late last evening from Loretta Lynch's chief of staff a copy of a 
proposed decision Lynch will release today reversing last Thursday's decision 
rejecting (0-5) retail price caps in San Diego.  The draft decision she 
proposes would establish an "interim" retail rate cap only for SDG&E 
residential and small commercial customers.  She proposes to use a "balancing 
account" to finance the cap.  Though it looks like the "interim" cap would 
extend through December 2003, there is one place in the decision that states 
the cap should only extend through December 2000.

In response to San Diego's complaint filed against all power sellers in 
California with market based rate authority, the Commission issued an order 
denying San Diego's request to cap all California power sellers' rates at 
$250.  However, the Commission in its order establishes a section 206 
proceeding to examine the justness and reasonableness of the rates of power 
sellers in the California markets.  Additionally, FERC is also ordering its 
staff to investigate whether the tariffs and institutional structures and 
bylaws of the California ISO and PX are adversely affecting the efficient 
operation of competitive wholesale electric power markets in California and 
need to be modified.

Wanted to make sure that you knew that today FERC declared the cap that the 
ISO Board voted out last week "null and void," which means that we're back to 
the old $250 cap.  FERC proposed a "soft" $150 cap that would take effect in 
60 days, however.  Call if you have questions.  Best, Jeff

Price caps have failed in the past and they'll fail again.
FERC's and California's immediate goal ought to be to make the bold reforms 
necessary to create real, competitive markets and eliminate the need for 
price caps altogether.
The most important reforms include:
Reforming California's siting laws to permit entry of supply---best way to 
undermine "high" prices is easy entry by competitors
Reforming the PUC review of utility purchases
Give the utilities financial incentives to purchase efficiently (i.e., 
similar to California's gas market, where a benchmark is set and the IOUs 
profit or lose on the basis of whether the IOU does better or worse than the 
benchmark).  It ain't rocket science, and it works.  
The CPUC gets out of the way and stops the practice of "after-the-fact" 
reviews of power purchases.
Creating a retail market
If California/FERC adopt these reforms, the need for caps will vanish.
FERC got a lot right in the order, but the price cap proposal is flawed.
Price is too low to incent development of peakers---well-functioning, 
efficient markets require peakers.
Information disclosure provisions are too costly and unnecessary.
Disincents energy efficiency.
IEP written comments will offer suggestions on how to remedy the flaws in the 
proposed cap.
